title: A neuron: weights, bias, activation
story:
A neuron is three operations and nothing else. It multiplies each input by a number, adds those products together along with one more number, and passes the result through a function. That is the whole unit, and everything built out of these is built only out of that.

Take the parts one at a time, because each has a job and the jobs are easy to confuse.

The weights say how much each input matters, and their signs say in which direction. A large positive weight means that raising the input raises the output; a large negative one means raising the input lowers it; a weight near zero means the input is being ignored. So the weights are where the learning ends up: training a network is adjusting these numbers, and nothing else about the unit changes.

The bias is the extra number added after the products, and it is the one people skip. Without it, every input being zero forces the sum to zero, which means the unit cannot represent anything that should be active in the absence of evidence. Geometrically the weighted sum defines a boundary, and the bias is what lets that boundary sit somewhere other than through the origin. Leaving it out does not make the unit slightly worse; it removes a degree of freedom the unit needs, and constrains every boundary it can draw to pass through one particular point.

The activation is the function applied at the end, and it is the only part that is not arithmetic on a straight line. Without it the unit computes a weighted sum plus a constant, which is a linear function — and this is the point that makes the rest of the subject possible: stacking linear functions gives a linear function. A hundred layers of weighted sums compute exactly what one layer of weighted sums computes. So the activation is not a refinement or a tuning choice. It is the only reason depth does anything at all.

What a single unit can express is worth being precise about, because it sets up why they are combined. The weighted sum with its bias divides the input space into two parts along a flat boundary, and the activation decides what the unit reports about which side an input falls on. That is genuinely useful and genuinely limited: any question whose answer cannot be settled by one flat boundary is outside a single unit, at every possible setting of its numbers.

Two things follow from that shape which are worth carrying forward. Because the unit is a weighted sum, the scale of the inputs matters — an input measured in large numbers will dominate one measured in small numbers before any learning has happened, purely because of the sizes involved. And because the weights are just numbers with no meaning attached, nothing distinguishes an important input from an unimportant one except what training discovers.

The reason to hold all of this precisely rather than approximately is that everything else in the subject is this unit repeated. When a network of millions of parameters does something surprising, the surprise is in the arrangement and the numbers, not in the parts. There is no additional mechanism hiding further in.

problem.name: The unit
problem.shape: A single output must be produced from several inputs, in a way that can be adjusted by training.
tell: a model is being described as though the unit does something more than arithmetic
the bias is omitted or treated as optional
inputs on wildly different scales are fed in unchanged
depth is being added without a non-linear step between layers
problem.move: Keep the three parts separate when reasoning: weights for how much each input matters and in which direction, the bias for where the boundary sits, and the activation for whether depth buys anything. Then check the input scales, because the unit is a weighted sum and sizes compete before training starts.
problem.invariant: Weighted sum plus bias is a linear function, and composing linear functions gives a linear function — so without a non-linear activation, any number of layers computes what one layer computes.
problem.breaks: A single unit divides the input space with one flat boundary, so any question not settled by one flat boundary is outside it at every setting of its numbers. That is a limit on what can be represented, not on what training can find, and no amount of data or patience reaches it.

cost.time: the non-linear step must be chosen, and the choice affects how well gradients move through a deep stack
cost.space: one weight per input per unit, which is where the parameter count comes from
cost.beats: a plain weighted sum, which is simpler and makes depth worthless, and a hand-written rule, which needs no training and requires you to already know the answer

problem.practice: Take two inputs and pick weights and a bias by hand so the unit answers yes when both inputs are large and no otherwise. Then try to pick weights and a bias so it answers yes when exactly one of them is large — and notice what stops you.

beats.broke: A unit that computes only a weighted sum is a linear function, and stacking linear functions gives a linear function — so depth built from them computes what a single layer computes.
beats.fix: Three parts with three jobs: weights for how much each input matters and in which direction, a bias so the boundary need not pass through the origin, and a non-linear activation so depth buys something.
beats.cost: One weight per input per unit is where the parameter count comes from, and because the unit is a weighted sum, inputs on different scales compete before any learning has happened.

interview.q: What does each of the three parts of a neuron do, and what happens if you leave one out?
interview.trap: Treating the activation as a tuning choice among several reasonable options. Without any non-linear step, depth is worthless — composing linear functions gives a linear function, so the activation is what makes layers mean anything.
interview.answer:
The weights say how much each input matters and in which direction — large positive raises the output with the input, large negative lowers it, near zero ignores it. This is where learning lands: training adjusts these numbers and nothing else about the unit changes.

The bias is the extra number added after the products, and omitting it is the most common mistake. Without it, all inputs being zero forces the sum to zero, so the unit cannot represent anything that should be active in the absence of evidence. Geometrically the weighted sum defines a boundary and the bias lets it sit somewhere other than through the origin — so leaving it out removes a degree of freedom and constrains every boundary the unit can draw to pass through one point.

The activation is the consequential omission. Without it the unit computes a weighted sum plus a constant, which is linear, and composing linear functions gives a linear function — so a hundred layers compute exactly what one layer computes. It is not a refinement; it is the only reason depth does anything, and a deep network without it is an expensive way to implement a shallow one.

On what one unit can express: the weighted sum with its bias divides the input space along one flat boundary, and the activation reports which side an input fell on. Any question not settled by one flat boundary is outside a single unit at every setting of its numbers — a limit on what can be represented rather than on what training can find, so no amount of data reaches it.

Two consequences of it being a weighted sum: input scale matters, because a large-valued input dominates a small-valued one before any learning has happened, which is why inputs get normalised; and the weights carry no meaning, so nothing marks an input as important except what training discovers.

I would end on why this is worth holding precisely: everything above it is this unit repeated, so when a large network does something surprising, the surprise is in the arrangement and the numbers. There is no further mechanism hiding deeper in.
